prompt: For unordered finite simple graph classes, what is the relation between bounded twin-width and bounded merge-width?

answers.text: Bounded twin-width implies bounded merge-width; the converse fails even for the class of graphs of maximum degree at most three.
answers.explanation: A bounded-red-degree contraction sequence gives bounds at each finite radius. Bounded-degree classes have bounded merge-width, while subcubic graphs have unbounded twin-width.

answers.text: Bounded merge-width implies bounded twin-width, but not conversely.
answers.explanation: The direction is reversed; the class of subcubic graphs refutes this implication.

answers.text: The two properties are equivalent for all unordered graph classes.
answers.explanation: Subcubic graphs give a counterexample to equivalence.
Bounded twin-width always implies bounded merge-width.

answers.text: The implication from twin-width to merge-width requires bounded clique-width as well.
answers.explanation: A bounded twin-width sequence suffices; no clique-width bound is needed.

answers.text: Bounded merge-width implies bounded twin-width whenever the class is hereditary.
answers.explanation: The class of all graphs of maximum degree at most three is hereditary and refutes this.

answers.text: Bounded merge-width implies bounded twin-width whenever the class has bounded maximum degree.
answers.explanation: Subcubic graphs have a fixed maximum-degree bound but unbounded twin-width.

answers.text: Bounded twin-width supplies one constant that bounds merge-width simultaneously at every radius, including infinity.
answers.explanation: A uniform infinity-radius bound would imply bounded clique-width, which square grids refute.

answers.text: Bounded twin-width supplies finite-radius merge-width bounds only after choosing an order as an extra input relation.
answers.explanation: The implication already holds for unordered graphs. An order is not required.

answers.text: The ordered-graph equivalence proves equivalence after simply forgetting the order on any bounded-merge-width graph.
answers.explanation: One must control the width of the ordered expansion. An unordered bound alone does not supply such an expansion.
